items.text: Understand what VPC peering is and why it's used instead of internet-based connectivity
Explain the request-accept model and why both parties must agree
Describe non-transitive routing and its implications for multi-VPC architectures
Know the CIDR overlap restriction — why overlapping ranges prevent peering
Explain edge-to-edge routing limitations (cannot use peer's IGW, VPN, NAT, or endpoints)
Understand ICMP and why it's used for network diagnostics (ping, traceroute)
Create a VPC peering connection (requester side) in the AWS Console
Accept a peering connection request (accepter side)
Add correct route table entries on both VPCs for bidirectional traffic
Configure Security Group rules to allow ICMP from a peered VPC's CIDR
Verify peering connectivity using ping from EC2 Instance Connect
Read CloudFormation templates to identify version pinning issues
Inspect RDS logs to diagnose database authentication failures
Can explain why route tables must be updated on BOTH sides of a peering connection
Know that VPC peering is non-transitive and what this means in practice
Understand when to choose Transit Gateway over VPC Peering (scale, hub-and-spoke)
Can calculate the number of peering connections needed for full mesh (N*(N-1)/2)
Know that security groups and NACLs still apply even with active peering
Validated CIDR blocks don't overlap using Python ipaddress module
Used `aws ec2 describe-vpcs` to inspect VPC CIDRs via CLI
Ran `ip route show` and understood the instance-level routing table
Tested DNS resolution with nslookup against the database endpoint
Confirmed port 3306 reachable with `nc -zv endpoint 3306`
Connected directly to database with mysql client and ran SHOW DATABASES
Used AWS CLI to inspect peering connection status and route tables
Simulated a routing failure by deleting a route — verified application broke
Restored the route and confirmed application recovered
Broke and fixed a security group rule — observed immediate traffic impact
Investigated Network ACL rules and understood stateless evaluation order
Enabled VPC Flow Logs and read ACCEPT/REJECT entries in CloudWatch
Calculated N×(N−1)÷2 connections for full mesh and compared with Transit Gateway
Created Application-VPC (10.0.0.0/16) with public subnet, IGW, and route table
Created Database-VPC (10.5.0.0/16) with private subnet and NO Internet Gateway
Created AppServer-SG and DBServer-SG with correct inbound rules
Launched App-Server (public IP) and DB-Server (private IP only)
Created App-DB-Peer peering connection and accepted it
Added peering routes to both VPC route tables
SSH'd from App-Server into DB-Server using its private IP
Started a Python HTTP server on DB-Server and called it from App-Server
Cleaned up all resources: instances terminated, peering deleted, VPCs removed
Can explain the full packet path from App-Server to DB-Server across VPC peering
Know the diagnostic order: peering status → routes → SG → NACL → DNS → port test
Understand why non-transitive routing matters and can give a real-world example
Can explain three business reasons to separate application and database into different VPCs
Can compare VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway and recommend the right one for a given scenario
Know the VPC peering cost model (no hourly charge, pay per GB transferred)
